item.title: GitHub CLI: Opt in to expiring, auto-refreshing OAuth tokens
item.dc:creator: Allison
item.description:
You can now use expiring, automatically refreshing OAuth credentials in GitHub CLI as part of a public preview. When you opt in, gh stores an expiring access token alongside a…

The post GitHub CLI: Opt in to expiring, auto-refreshing OAuth tokens appeared first on The GitHub Blog.
item.content:encoded:
You can now use expiring, automatically refreshing OAuth credentials in GitHub CLI as part of a public preview. When you opt in, gh stores an expiring access token alongside a rotating refresh token and automatically refreshes the token whenever it is needed. You stay authenticated without reauthenticating, and a leaked access token becomes unusable within hours instead of lasting indefinitely.

Opting in at login

Starting with v2.103.0, pass the new --expiring flag when you log in with gh auth login --expiring. To opt in for every sign-in without passing the flag each time, run gh config set expiring_credentials enabled. From then on, there is nothing new to run day to day: gh refreshes the credential for you in the background. To check the state of an expiring credential, including when the current access token expires, run gh auth status.

Using expiring tokens with git

If you authenticate to git over HTTPS and want to use expiring tokens, we strongly recommend configuring gh as your git credential helper by running gh auth setup-git. This lets gh serve and refresh the credential for git, so your expiring token is correctly handled.

We also strongly recommend upgrading to git 2.46 or newer, which lets gh mark expiring credentials so they are not cached past their lifetime. On older git versions, gh still works but prints a one-time recommendation to upgrade.

Good to know

  • It’s opt-in and backward compatible. If you don’t opt in through the flag or configuration setting, nothing changes. Existing sign-ins and manually supplied tokens keep working exactly as before.
  • You get whatever the server issues. --expiring requests refreshable credentials. If a server does not support them, gh falls back cleanly to a normal nonexpiring token.
  • It will become the default over time. Expiring credentials are opt-in today. In a future release, we plan to make them the default for new sign-ins.

Things to watch out for

Expiring access tokens are short-lived, so anything that captures a token once and reuses it later can break. Scripts and extensions that run gh auth token and store the result, or copy the token into another tool, will eventually be left holding an expired token.

If you consume the token outside of gh, read it fresh each time with gh auth token. This refreshes it when needed rather than caching the value. If a workflow depends on a token that stays valid for a long time, hold off on opting in for that workflow. When gh is configured as your git credential helper, it refreshes the credential for you, so git operations over HTTPS keep working.

Who can use it

Expiring tokens are available on github.com and ghe.com today. GitHub Enterprise Server issues them starting with GHES 3.23. On earlier versions, opting in falls back to today’s nonexpiring behavior.

For more on authenticating with GitHub CLI, including expiring tokens, see Authenticating with GitHub CLI.

Install or upgrade to GitHub CLI v2.103.0 today to get started.

Have feedback or found an issue? Open an issue in the cli/cli repository.

The post GitHub CLI: Opt in to expiring, auto-refreshing OAuth tokens appeared first on The GitHub Blog.

item.title: Bulk migrate branch protections to rulesets for a repository
item.dc:creator: Allison
item.description:
You can now convert all branch protection rules of a repository to rulesets in a single action. This is an extension of the ability to convert a single branch protection…

The post Bulk migrate branch protections to rulesets for a repository appeared first on The GitHub Blog.
item.content:encoded:
You can now convert all branch protection rules of a repository to rulesets in a single action. This is an extension of the ability to convert a single branch protection rule to a ruleset that we released previously, now allowing for at-scale conversions.

How it works

Navigate to Settings → Rulesets in your repository and click Import branch protection rules. In the Review import dialog, you can:

  • Preview the rulesets that will be created before you confirm the conversion.
  • See which branch protection rules are already covered by an existing ruleset.
  • Review cases where one branch protection rule produces multiple rulesets to preserve its original behavior.
  • Choose an enforcement status (e.g., Active, Evaluate, or Disabled) and select which rulesets to create.

After you click Create rulesets, choose whether to keep or delete the original branch protection rules.

Why migrate to rulesets?

Rulesets offer several advantages over classic branch protections:

  • Apply rules across multiple branches with pattern matching
  • Layer multiple rulesets for granular policy control
  • Manage rulesets at the organization or enterprise level
  • Configure fine-grained bypass permissions for users, teams, and apps

Availability

This feature is available for all repositories where rulesets are available. Learn more about converting your branch protections to repository rulesets.

Join the discussion within GitHub Community.

The post Bulk migrate branch protections to rulesets for a repository appeared first on The GitHub Blog.

item.title: Updates to GitHub secret scanning
item.dc:creator: Allison
item.description:
This update covers improvements and bug fixes for GitHub secret scanning. Update to audit log events On November 12, 2026, the business field in affected secret_scanning_alert.* and secret_scanning_push_protection.bypass audit log…

The post Updates to GitHub secret scanning appeared first on The GitHub Blog.
item.content:encoded:
This update covers improvements and bug fixes for GitHub secret scanning.

Update to audit log events

On November 12, 2026, the business field in affected secret_scanning_alert.* and secret_scanning_push_protection.bypass audit log events will change from the enterprise display name to the enterprise slug.

To avoid disruption to any automated workflows, you should update integrations that filter by display name before rollout to accept both formats or use business_id instead. The business field remains a string. Event names and numeric business_id values are unchanged.

Recent improvements and bug fixes

  • Custom pattern alerts: Existing open alerts stay open when a rescan finds that they still match an edited custom pattern, rather than being closed and reopened.
  • Base64-encoded GitHub tokens: In private and internal repositories on github.com with secret scanning enabled, the existing revocation action (public preview) now supports encoded personal access tokens (classic), fine-grained personal access tokens, OAuth access tokens, and GitHub App user access tokens. GitHub automatically decodes the value.
  • Dismissal-request webhooks: Payloads now include exemption_request.number, the repository-scoped request number also available in the REST API. Use the repository and request number together to correlate requests across integrations.
  • Accessibility: The Request pending status on an alert is now keyboard-focusable without activating an action. The revocation flow announces progress to screen readers and moves focus to its completion panel when that panel appears.
  • Bypass-request metadata: Fixed empty secret-type and location details in bypass-request API responses and webhook payloads for command-line pushes when another repository rule ran after secret scanning.
  • Delegated bypass: Fixed push failures caused by existing organization-role entries in reviewer lists, and 500 errors when setting valid reviewer configurations for organization-owned repositories through the REST API.
  • Custom pattern API: Requests rejected by the scanning service for invalid arguments now return 422 instead of 500, so your integration can distinguish these input errors from server failures.

Learn more

Learn more about enterprise audit log events and the secret scanning REST API. Share your feedback in GitHub Community.

The post Updates to GitHub secret scanning appeared first on The GitHub Blog.

item.title: Dependabot alerts REST API now includes dependency versions
item.dc:creator: Allison
item.description:
You can now get the version of a vulnerable dependency directly from Dependabot alert responses in the REST API. Each alert’s dependency object includes a new version_requirement field with the…

The post Dependabot alerts REST API now includes dependency versions appeared first on The GitHub Blog.
item.content:encoded:
You can now get the version of a vulnerable dependency directly from Dependabot alert responses in the REST API. Each alert’s dependency object includes a new version_requirement field with the version or version constraint that Dependabot last recorded for the alert.

Alert responses already included the advisory’s vulnerable version range, but not the version in your repository. If you sync alerts to other security tools, you no longer need to parse lockfiles or make a separate GraphQL request for vulnerableRequirements to get that version.

The value depends on how Dependabot detected the dependency:

  • Lockfiles: The resolved version.
  • Manifests without a lockfile: The version or version constraint declared in the manifest.
  • Dependency submission API: The resolved version submitted by your build tooling.

The field is null when no value is available. If an alert covers more than one vulnerable version of a dependency, the field holds one recorded value and may not represent all of them. Long version constraints may also be truncated.

You’ll find version_requirement in responses for individual alerts, in repository, organization, and enterprise alert lists, and in dependabot_alert webhook payloads.

This field is available now on github.com and GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency, and will be included in GitHub Enterprise Server 3.24.

Learn more about the REST API endpoints for Dependabot alerts and the dependabot_alert webhook event.

The post Dependabot alerts REST API now includes dependency versions appeared first on The GitHub Blog.

item.title: GitHub package firewall in public preview
item.dc:creator: Allison
item.description:
Editor’s note (October 21, 2026): Rewrote the changelog for clarity and added imagery. There’s been a recent flood of malware attacks that exploit systems at package installation time. Agents and…

The post GitHub package firewall in public preview appeared first on The GitHub Blog.
item.content:encoded:
Editor’s note (October 21, 2026): Rewrote the changelog for clarity and added imagery.

There’s been a recent flood of malware attacks that exploit systems at package installation time. Agents and CI runners are particularly vulnerable to these attacks because they install dependencies to accomplish a task or complete a build without a human in the loop. To stem this tide, GitHub is introducing a new package firewall, which sits between endpoints or internal registries and the upstream package repositories. The firewall inspects both metadata requests and package downloads for signs of malicious activity, acting as an install-time policy gate. The package firewall is available today in public preview for all GitHub Enterprise Cloud customers, including data-resident GitHub Enterprise Cloud.

How it works

First, administrators set policy controls for their enterprise. The controls available today include a configurable cooldown period, checking the GitHub Advisory Database for malware or vulnerability advisories, and supply-chain checks like attestation downgrades.

Then, endpoints like coding agents and CI/CD hosts use the firewall for their requests instead of pointing directly at the upstream package registries. Metadata requests for package lists as well as the actual package downloads flow through the firewall, which evaluates them against the policy. If a package is blocked erroneously, the user can request an exception with a workflow similar to other GitHub Advanced Security features.

Availability and limitations

The package firewall is available in public preview as we scale up the infrastructure behind it and continue to add features based on customer demand. It is available to GitHub Enterprise Cloud customers, including GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency. The service is free while in the preview period. When it reaches general availability, it will be charged based on metered usage, similar to Actions billing.

Currently the package firewall only supports npm packages.

How to use it

For detailed setup instructions, see Protecting endpoints with package firewall. Join the discussion in GitHub Community.

The post GitHub package firewall in public preview appeared first on The GitHub Blog.

item.title: Dependabot now supports npm 12, pnpm 11 and 12, and Bun 1.4
item.dc:creator: Allison
item.description:
You can now upgrade your projects to npm 12, pnpm 11 or 12, or Bun 1.4 and keep receiving Dependabot updates. Support for these package manager versions is available to…

The post Dependabot now supports npm 12, pnpm 11 and 12, and Bun 1.4 appeared first on The GitHub Blog.
item.content:encoded:
You can now upgrade your projects to npm 12, pnpm 11 or 12, or Bun 1.4 and keep receiving Dependabot updates. Support for these package manager versions is available to all github.com users and will be included in GitHub Enterprise Server 3.24.

For the full list of package manager versions that Dependabot supports, see Dependabot supported ecosystems and repositories.

Known limitation: When pnpm writes pnpm-lock.yaml as two YAML documents (the pnpm 12 default for projects that pin a pnpm version), the dependency graph doesn’t detect the dependencies in that file yet. Dependabot version updates still work, but Dependabot alerts and security updates won’t be created for those dependencies, and existing alerts for them may close. We’re working on adding support.

The post Dependabot now supports npm 12, pnpm 11 and 12, and Bun 1.4 appeared first on The GitHub Blog.

item.title: Copilot model policy API for enterprise, orgs, and teams
item.dc:creator: Allison
item.description:
You can now use the REST API to retrieve and update Copilot model policies for enterprises, enterprise teams, agent apps, and organizations. What’s new GET and PATCH endpoints are now…

The post Copilot model policy API for enterprise, orgs, and teams appeared first on The GitHub Blog.
item.content:encoded:
You can now use the REST API to retrieve and update Copilot model policies for enterprises, enterprise teams, agent apps, and organizations.

What’s new

GET and PATCH endpoints are now generally available for model policies at four levels:

  • Enterprise: /enterprises/{enterprise}/copilot/model-policies
  • Enterprise teams: /enterprises/{enterprise}/teams/{team_slug}/copilot/model-policies
  • Agent apps: /enterprises/{enterprise}/copilot/apps/model-policies
  • Organization: /orgs/{org}/copilot/model-policies

Together, these endpoints make it easier to manage Copilot model availability across your enterprise. Enterprise policies can delegate model control to organizations in organization mode, or to teams and apps in enterprise teams mode. Reference our documentation on managing availability of models in your enterprise and our REST API documentation to get started.

The post Copilot model policy API for enterprise, orgs, and teams appeared first on The GitHub Blog.

item.title: GitHub Copilot models deprecated on October 19, 2026
item.dc:creator: Allison
item.description:
As of today, October 19, 2026, we have deprecated the following models across most GitHub Copilot experiences (including Copilot Chat, inline edits, ask and agent modes, and code completions). These…

The post GitHub Copilot models deprecated on October 19, 2026 appeared first on The GitHub Blog.
item.content:encoded:
As of today, October 19, 2026, we have deprecated the following models across most GitHub Copilot experiences (including Copilot Chat, inline edits, ask and agent modes, and code completions).

These deprecations were announced on September 18, 2026.

Model Deprecation date Suggested alternative
Gemini 3.7 Flash 2026-10-19 Gemini 3.8 Flash
GPT-5.5 2026-10-19 GPT-6.1 Sol
GPT-5.4 2026-10-19 GPT-6.1 Sol
GPT-5.4 mini 2026-10-19 GPT-6 Luna
GPT-5 mini 2026-10-19 GPT-6 Luna
Grok 4.5 2026-10-19 Grok 4.7

Please update your workflows and integrations to use supported models. Copilot Enterprise administrators may need to enable access to alternative models through their model policies in Copilot settings. As an administrator, you can verify availability by checking your individual Copilot settings and confirming that the policy is enabled for the specific model. Once enabled, you’ll see the model in the Copilot Chat model selector in VS Code and on github.com. No action is required to remove the deprecated models.

GitHub Enterprise customers with questions or concerns are encouraged to reach out to their account manager for further assistance.

Share your feedback

To learn more about the models available in Copilot, see our documentation on models and get started with Copilot today.

Join the GitHub Community to share your feedback.

item.title: Some Git over HTTPS may temporarily require authentication
item.dc:creator: Allison
item.description:
During periods of unusual traffic, GitHub may temporarily require authentication for some clones and fetches of public repositories over HTTPS to help protect github.com’s availability. If an operation is affected,…

The post Some Git over HTTPS may temporarily require authentication appeared first on The GitHub Blog.
item.content:encoded:
During periods of unusual traffic, GitHub may temporarily require authentication for some clones and fetches of public repositories over HTTPS to help protect github.com’s availability. If an operation is affected, it will fail with a message indicating that authentication is required.

To continue, authenticate and retry the operation. You can also wait and retry without authentication after the temporary protection has been lifted.

GitHub applies this protection as narrowly as possible using signals associated with anomalous traffic. Because legitimate and anomalous traffic can sometimes share those signals, legitimate unauthenticated operations may occasionally be affected. This is not a general authentication requirement for public repositories.

The following operations are unaffected:

  • Authenticated Git operations over HTTPS
  • Git operations over SSH
  • Pushes
  • Unrelated GitHub web and API traffic

For more reliable automated clones and fetches, configure authentication:

  • GitHub Actions: Use the built-in GITHUB_TOKEN.
  • Other CI systems: Prefer a GitHub App installation access token. A personal access token can also be used.
  • Operations that cannot authenticate: Retry after the temporary protection has been lifted.

This protection applies to repositories on github.com across all plans.

For setup instructions, see about authentication to GitHub and managing remote repositories.

The post Some Git over HTTPS may temporarily require authentication appeared first on The GitHub Blog.

item.title: CodeQL changes for macOS 27, Xcode 27, and Swift 6.4
item.dc:creator: Allison
item.description:
Starting with macOS 27 and Xcode 27, Apple no longer includes Intel (x86_64) code in some of the system binaries and libraries that CodeQL relies on to trace builds. As…

The post CodeQL changes for macOS 27, Xcode 27, and Swift 6.4 appeared first on The GitHub Blog.
item.content:encoded:
Starting with macOS 27 and Xcode 27, Apple no longer includes Intel (x86_64) code in some of the system binaries and libraries that CodeQL relies on to trace builds. As a result, CodeQL can’t support traced scans on these versions or analyze Swift 6.4.

What’s affected

  • Xcode 27: When Xcode 27 is installed, traced extraction isn’t available for C/C++, C#, Go, Java, Kotlin, or Swift.
  • macOS 27: Traced extraction may not be available for the previously mentioned languages.
  • Swift 6.4: CodeQL doesn’t support Swift 6.4 on any platform.
  • Intel-based Macs: CodeQL support for Intel-based Macs will be deprecated in mid-December 2026.

How to keep your scans running

If you scan Swift or use traced builds for other languages, pin your workflows to macOS 26 or earlier and Xcode 26 or earlier. If you use GitHub Actions, pin the runner image and toolchain in your workflow rather than relying on the latest versions.

For C/C++, C#, and Java, you can switch to build mode none, which doesn’t require tracing a build.

Join the discussion within GitHub Community.

The post CodeQL changes for macOS 27, Xcode 27, and Swift 6.4 appeared first on The GitHub Blog.
